audience.programmeDescription: Groningen History studies the past from antiquity to the present. Students learn to interpret sources, study regions and communicate historical research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options explore historical questions through culture and memory, politics and conflict, or economy and society. Groningen follows a continuous History curriculum and requires a thesis.

cellNotes.text: Both survey major political, economic and social changes of the twentieth century. UCR begins its survey in 1815.
Both study ancient societies. UCR focuses on archaeology and material culture.
UCR studies Renaissance art, trade and exchange in the Mediterranean, one part of Groningen’s broader survey.
Both examine historical power and political organisation. UCR compares empires across periods and regions.
Both examine how scholars interpret the past. UCR focuses on the history of art history.
Both develop regional historical inquiry and public communication. UCR works with Indigenous histories and multimedia.
Groningen surveys the Middle Ages in a dedicated course. UCR studies parts of the period through empire, war and art.
Groningen studies Dutch history in a global context in a dedicated course.
Groningen introduces the methods of historical research before students start the thematic seminars.
Groningen requires a research seminar in social and economic history. UCR combines history, economics and sociology across several courses.
Groningen requires a 10 EC thesis. UCR’s American Century course develops historical research through a course paper, and optional independent research sits outside the illustrated schedules.

notes.text: Groningen teaches a continuous History curriculum from antiquity through the present, including dedicated seminars, regional research and a required thesis. The UCR options combine history with courses in culture, politics or economics and society. Their period coverage and research requirements differ.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

source.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.text: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.

source.reviewNote: CP076: full selected description read against current course evidence; accurate bounded official overview. Retain unchanged text, without adding unstated methods or qualifications.

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.text: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.

source.reviewNote: CP076: full selected description read against current course evidence; accurate bounded official overview. Retain unchanged text, without adding unstated methods or qualifications.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

source.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

source.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.text: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

source.reviewNote: CP076: full selected description read against current course evidence; accurate bounded official overview. Retain unchanged text, without adding unstated methods or qualifications.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.text: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

source.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.text: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.text: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.

source.reviewNote: Read the unchanged display text against the current official description and actual course evidence. It accurately conveys the supported historical, heritage, museum or material-media focus without claiming archaeological field qualification. No displayed text changed.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

source.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.text: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.text: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.text: Introduction to Public International Law examines its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic law. Topics include responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection, followed by self-determination, Third World approaches, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises and a research podcast develop legal reasoning and critical analysis.

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.text: Comparative Constitutional Law compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students study federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review, human rights, public participation and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and hypothetical cases.

GOSLAWJ312.text: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.text: Introduction to Political Philosophy examines political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.text: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.text: Theory of International Relations introduces competing approaches to international relations and geopolitics, including realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism and critical theory. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases. A United Nations Security Council simulation develops country-position research, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.text: European Union Politics examines EU institutions, actors, integration and policymaking, including representation, legitimacy and decision-making. An empirical project investigates European Parliament committee amendments, relating MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.text: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.text: Peace & Conflict examines conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.

Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

MCCCOMM111.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

MCCCOMM213.text: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.text: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.text: Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.text: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.text: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.text: Film & Text studies relationships between literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality. Students learn methods of film analysis and examine plot, character, setting, image, acting, music and sound, alongside the relationships among adaptors, critics and viewers.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.text: Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
